models.name: age_seir
models.title: Age-structured SEIR with contact matrices
models.summary: SEIR over age groups mixing through a contact matrix, as binomial cohorts.

card.name: age_seir
card.title: Age-structured SEIR with contact matrices
card.summary: An SEIR epidemic over age groups that mix through a contact matrix, written as binomial cohorts so a million people cost what a hundred do.
intended_use: Teaching how age mixing shapes an epidemic: attack rates by group, the role of the contact matrix, R0 as a spectral radius.
A starting point for age-structured epidemic models, with a validated core to extend (vaccination, interventions on contacts).
Comparing scenarios in relative terms (contact reductions in one group against another) on a stated contact matrix.
out_of_scope: Forecasting a real epidemic: the default contact matrix is illustrative, not survey data, and nothing is calibrated.
Decisions about a specific population without a contact matrix measured on it (social-contact surveys, or `scenario_from_population`).
Diseases whose natural history is not SEIR with geometric periods (waning immunity, asymptomatic carriers, age-dependent severity).
data: None by default: group sizes, the 3 x 3 contact matrix and the rates are illustrative values in `SEIRScenario`.
Optionally, a synthetic population from census tables (`modelly.population`), from which `scenario_from_population` takes group sizes and measures the contact matrix.
limits: Homogeneous mixing within each age group: no households, places or networks, so local saturation and clustering are absent.
One step is one unit of time with transitions drawn once per step; the exposed and infectious periods are geometric, not fixed or gamma-distributed.
Closed population: no births, deaths or migration, so runs longer than one epidemic wave are not meaningful.
The final-size check validates the transmission core, not the time course: peak timing depends on the step and the periods.
ethics: Age-targeted results (who to protect or restrict first) affect real groups; present them with their intervals and with the assumptions above, never as a forecast.
An illustrative contact matrix can make one age group look responsible for spread; say where the matrix comes from whenever results are shown.

validation.check: attack rate within five standard deviations of the final-size relation (one group and three equal groups, three seeds)
each age group's attack rate against the multi-group final-size relation
with vaccinated people in one group, each group's attack rate follows the final-size relation without them
an outbreak with R0 below one stays small; nobody is created or lost; same seed, same epidemic

references: Kermack, W. O. and McKendrick, A. G. (1927). A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 115, 700-721.
Mossong, J. et al. (2008). Social contacts and mixing patterns relevant to the spread of infectious diseases. PLoS Medicine, 5(3), e74.
Andersson, H. and Britton, T. (2000). Stochastic Epidemic Models and Their Statistical Analysis. Lecture Notes in Statistics 151, Springer.

models.name: within_host
models.title: Within-host and between-host epidemic
models.summary: Hosts infect each other; each infection is a viral ODE inside its host.

card.name: within_host
card.title: Within-host and between-host epidemic
card.summary: Hosts infect each other while each infection runs as a target-cell-limited viral ODE inside its host, all hosts integrated as one batch with each host's own solve_ivp steps.
intended_use: Teaching how within-host dynamics (viral growth, a threshold for infectiousness) shape an epidemic between hosts.
A starting point for nested models: per-host treatment, immunity or dose effects on top of a validated viral core.
Showing per-agent ODEs with events at scale: onsets and clearances located to the instant for a hundred thousand hosts.
out_of_scope: Forecasting an influenza season or any real outbreak: contacts and transmissibility are illustrative and nothing is calibrated to case data.
Clinical questions about individual patients: the viral parameters are of the order fitted for influenza A, in relative units, not a patient's.
Infections with a latent reservoir, an immune response or reinfection, which the three-equation model does not have.
data: None by default: the viral rates are of the order Baccam et al. (2006) fitted for influenza A, in relative units, and the contact parameters in `WithinHostScenario` are illustrative.
The infection rate of each host is drawn from a lognormal law with the scenario's median and spread, from the model's seed.
limits: Homogeneous mixing between hosts: the chance of exposure depends only on the share infectious, with no households, places or networks.
Infectiousness is all or nothing at a virus threshold; transmission does not grow with the load.
No immune response: a host's infection ends only when its target cells are used up, and an exposed host is never exposed again.
Exposure happens once a day in the transmission phase; only the course of each infection is continuous in time.
ethics: Results about who becomes infectious when could be read as advice on isolation periods; they rest on illustrative parameters and must not be presented as such.
Host-to-host variation comes from a drawn infection rate, not from data on people; say so when the spread of outcomes between hosts is shown.

validation.check: one day of the whole population equals one solve_ivp call per exposed host, final states and onset times, to round-off
with no target cells the virus clears at log(V0 / threshold) / c, to a relative 1e-6, for fifty initial loads
cells stay in [0, 1]; an outbreak needs contacts; same seed same outbreak, straight or resumed from a checkpoint

references: Baccam, P., Beauchemin, C., Macken, C. A., Hayden, F. G. and Perelson, A. S. (2006). Kinetics of influenza A virus infection in humans. Journal of Virology, 80(15), 7590-7599.
Hairer, E., Norsett, S. P. and Wanner, G. (1993). Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I: Nonstiff Problems, 2nd ed. Springer.
Mideo, N., Alizon, S. and Day, T. (2008). Linking within- and between-host dynamics in the evolutionary epidemiology of infectious diseases. Trends in Ecology and Evolution, 23(9), 511-517.

models.name: vector_borne
models.title: Vector-borne transmission on a landscape
models.summary: Ross-Macdonald transmission between moving hosts and mosquito cohorts per cell.

card.name: vector_borne
card.title: Vector-borne transmission on a landscape
card.summary: Ross-Macdonald transmission between hosts that move on a landscape grid and mosquitoes held as binomial cohorts per cell, with an optional habitat raster setting where the mosquitoes are.
intended_use: Teaching the Ross-Macdonald model: how vector density, biting rate, mosquito survival and incubation combine into R0, and why R0 is linear in the density `m`.
Exploring in relative terms how a habitat raster and host movement shape where and how far an outbreak spreads.
A starting point for vector-borne models on real landscapes, with a validated transmission core to extend (vector control, seasonality, more host states).
out_of_scope: Forecasting a real malaria, dengue or other vector-borne outbreak: the bionomics are illustrative and nothing is calibrated.
Planning vector control for a specific place without entomological data measured there (densities, biting and survival rates, habitat).
Diseases with a host latent period, waning immunity, several vector species or human-to-human transmission, none of which the model has.
data: None by default: the 10 x 10 landscape, 20 hosts per cell and the daily rates are illustrative values in `VectorScenario`.
Optionally, a habitat suitability raster of shape `(width, height)`, for example the values of a `modelly.space.geo.RasterLayer`, passed as `habitat`.
limits: Mosquitoes do not move between cells and bite only hosts of their own cell, chosen at random; hosts move to a random neighbouring cell.
One step is one day with every transition drawn once per step, so the infectious and incubation periods are geometric.
Emergence keeps the vector density at `m`: no seasonality, weather or density dependence in the mosquito population.
Closed host population with no births, deaths or loss of immunity; the validation orders outbreak sizes by R0, it does not check the time course.
ethics: Results about where an outbreak spreads can steer spraying, bed-net or other resources towards some communities and away from others; present them as illustrative, with the assumptions above.
A habitat raster can make one area look like the source of transmission; say where the raster comes from whenever results are shown.

validation.check: R0 is linear in the vector density, below one at m = 0.5 and above one at m = 2 and 4, and matches the Ross-Macdonald formula
attack rates come out in the order of R0 for three seeds: under 5 % when R0 < 1, over 80 % at R0 about 4
a habitat raster confines the mosquitoes; hosts are conserved; same seed, same epidemic

references: Ross, R. (1911). The Prevention of Malaria, 2nd ed. John Murray.
Macdonald, G. (1957). The Epidemiology and Control of Malaria. Oxford University Press.

models.name: habitat_selection
models.title: Habitat selection on a real land-cover raster
models.summary: Animals disperse over ESA WorldCover land cover and settle where it suits them.

card.name: habitat_selection
card.title: Habitat selection on a real land-cover raster
card.summary: Animals disperse over a land-cover raster by a Metropolis rule weighted by a preference per land-cover class, and settle in proportion to habitat quality and area.
intended_use: Teaching the link between movement and habitat use: a Metropolis walk whose stationary law is the resource-selection-function view of occupancy.
A starting point for dispersal models on real land cover, with any `RasterLayer`'s values in place of the bundled window.
Comparing in relative terms how preference weights and jump radius change occupancy across land-cover classes.
out_of_scope: Predicting where a real species lives: the default weights describe an illustrative woodland species and are not fitted to any species.
Conservation or land-use decisions without preference weights estimated from data on the species in question.
Questions about population dynamics, territories or interactions between animals: the animals are independent and never born or die.
data: A bundled 120 x 120 window of ESA WorldCover 2021 at 10 m over the Intervale in Burlington, Vermont (CC BY 4.0, © ESA WorldCover project 2021); its source and checksum are in `modelly/space/geo/data/NOTICE.md`. Reading it needs the `geo` extra.
Preference weights per class are illustrative values (`WOODLAND` in the model); any `(width, height)` land-cover array can replace the raster through `cover`.
limits: Animals are independent: no density dependence, competition or social behaviour, so occupancy depends only on the weights and the cover.
Movement is a symmetric jump within a square of side `2 * radius + 1` accepted by the Metropolis rule, not a model of real movement paths or barriers between cells.
Weights depend on the land-cover class alone, not on distance to edges, patch size or neighbouring classes.
The validation checks the stationary law, not how fast animals reach it on a given raster.
ethics: Occupancy maps can be read as statements about where a species needs protection; with illustrative weights they say nothing about any real species, so say so whenever they are shown.

validation.check: from a uniform start far from the law, every class share is within five multinomial standard deviations of the stationary law (three seeds)
a population started at the law stays within that bound at every step
a class of weight 0 is never entered; equal weights give area shares; same seed, same walk

references: Metropolis, N., Rosenbluth, A. W., Rosenbluth, M. N., Teller, A. H. and Teller, E. (1953). Equation of state calculations by fast computing machines. Journal of Chemical Physics, 21(6), 1087-1092.
Manly, B. F. J., McDonald, L. L., Thomas, D. L., McDonald, T. L. and Erickson, W. P. (2002). Resource Selection by Animals, 2nd ed. Kluwer.
Zanaga, D. et al. (2022). ESA WorldCover 10 m 2021 v200. Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.7254221.

models.name: hospital_epidemic
models.title: Epidemic coupled to hospital capacity
models.summary: SIR agents whose admissions drive a hospital stock-flow ODE that damps contacts.

card.name: hospital_epidemic
card.title: Epidemic coupled to hospital capacity
card.summary: SIR agents whose severe cases fill a hospital stock-flow model that opens surge beds, while the pressure on beds feeds back to lower contacts.
intended_use: Teaching how an agent-based epidemic couples to a system-dynamics model: admissions flow one way, bed pressure the other, with a lag of one step.
Comparing scenarios in relative terms: how surge capacity, length of stay or the strength of the contact response change peak occupancy and the attack rate.
A starting point for epidemic and health-system models, with a validated epidemic core, an exactly checked hospital and a closed mass balance.
out_of_scope: Forecasting bed demand for a real hospital or health system: the rates, the severe share and the bed numbers are illustrative and nothing is calibrated.
Capacity or triage decisions for a specific hospital without its own admission, stay and staffing data.
Epidemics whose natural history is not SIR with geometric periods, or where severity depends on age or other attributes.
data: None by default: the population of 20,000, the transmission and recovery rates, the 2 % severe share and the hospital parameters are illustrative values in `HospitalScenario`.
limits: Homogeneous mixing: no households, places or networks, and everyone responds to bed pressure in the same way.
Admitted patients only occupy beds and are discharged at rate `occupied / stay`; there are no deaths, no staff limits and no turned-away patients when beds run out.
One step is one unit of time with transitions drawn once per step, and the hospital sees each step's admissions held constant over that step.
Closed population with no births, deaths or waning immunity; the final-size check holds only without the contact response.
ethics: Results about bed capacity and contact reductions bear on decisions that affect patients and health workers; present them as illustrative, with the assumptions above, never as a forecast.
The contact response is one illustrative rule; do not read it as a measured behaviour of any population.

validation.check: without the response, the attack rate is within five standard deviations of the final-size relation (three seeds)
occupancy and beds match the exact matrix-exponential solution within 1e-6, with and without the response
admissions equal patients in hospital plus those discharged, to round-off, and beds equal base beds plus the net amount opened
a stronger response lowers peak occupancy and the attack rate; people are conserved; a resumed checkpoint is identical; same seed, same run

references: Kermack, W. O. and McKendrick, A. G. (1927). A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 115, 700-721.
Andersson, H. and Britton, T. (2000). Stochastic Epidemic Models and Their Statistical Analysis. Lecture Notes in Statistics 151, Springer.
Sterman, J. D. (2000). Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World. Irwin/McGraw-Hill.

models.name: energy_budget
models.title: Individual-based population with energy budgets
models.summary: Foragers that eat, pay a metabolic cost, reproduce and starve on a resource grid.

card.name: energy_budget
card.title: Individual-based population with energy budgets
card.summary: Foragers that walk a resource grid, eat, pay a metabolic cost, reproduce by splitting their energy and starve, so the energy balance sets the carrying capacity.
intended_use: Teaching how an energy budget regulates an individual-based population, and how the carrying capacity follows from inflow, efficiency and cost.
A starting point for individual-based ecology models with a validated energy core to extend (age, spatial variation in inflow, predators).
Comparing in relative terms how resource inflow, assimilation efficiency or metabolic cost move the equilibrium population.
out_of_scope: Predicting the abundance of a real species: the parameters are illustrative and nothing is calibrated.
Management decisions such as harvest or stocking levels for a real population.
Questions that depend on age, sex, size or behaviour beyond a random walk, none of which the foragers have.
data: None by default: the 30 x 30 grid, the inflow, efficiency, cost and birth threshold are illustrative values in `EnergyScenario`.
limits: Foragers move to a random neighbouring cell every step and do not seek food; the foragers in a cell share its resource equally.
The resource is never capped and is eaten whenever a forager visits, which is what makes the long-run intake equal the inflow.
Reproduction is a split of energy at a fixed threshold, with no age, mates or maturation; death comes only from starvation.
The validation checks the mean population against the carrying capacity, not the size or period of fluctuations around it.
ethics: This is a teaching model with no real population behind it; results carry no direct consequences for people, but say it is illustrative if they are used to argue about a real population.

validation.check: mean population after a burn-in of 150 steps is within 3 % of the carrying capacity from the energy balance (three seeds, two inflows)
after the burn-in the uneaten resource stock does not grow: its mean over the second half is within 5 % of the first half
without inflow the population dies out; energy columns stay in range and follow the agents; same seed, same population curve

references: Grimm, V. and Railsback, S. F. (2005). Individual-based Modeling and Ecology. Princeton University Press.

models.name: nutrient_foragers
models.title: Foragers on a diffusing nutrient field
models.summary: Foragers eat from a nutrient that enters at a river bank and diffuses inland.

card.name: nutrient_foragers
card.title: Foragers on a diffusing nutrient field
card.summary: Foragers eat from a nutrient that enters along a river bank, diffuses inland and decays, coupled to the field so that the energy balance sets the carrying capacity.
intended_use: Teaching how agents couple to a diffusing field: the foragers' phase writes what was eaten, the field adds it and diffuses one phase later.
Showing how the energy balance sets a carrying capacity that does not depend on how far the nutrient diffuses, and how decay takes its share.
A starting point for consumer-resource models on a spatial field, with a closed nutrient budget to keep when extending it.
out_of_scope: Predicting real nutrient concentrations or consumer densities along a river: the supply, diffusion and decay are illustrative and nothing is calibrated.
Water-quality or land-management decisions for a real catchment.
Systems where the nutrient is carried by flow (advection) or leaves through the boundaries: the landscape is closed and the field only diffuses and decays.
data: None by default: the 20 x 20 grid, the supply along the western edge, the diffusion coefficient and the forager parameters are illustrative values in `NutrientScenario`.
limits: Foragers move to a random neighbouring cell and do not climb the nutrient gradient; the density pattern comes from the field alone.
The nutrient enters only along the western edge at a constant rate, with closed walls elsewhere and no seasonality.
Reproduction is a split of energy at a fixed threshold, with no age or maturation; death comes only from starvation.
The validation checks the mean population against the energy balance, not the size of fluctuations or the transient approach to it.
ethics: This is a teaching model with no real system behind it; results carry no direct consequences for people, but say it is illustrative if they are used to argue about a real river or population.

validation.check: without decay, the mean population after a burn-in of 150 steps is within 3 % of the carrying capacity (three seeds)
the mean population is within 1 % of the energy balance with the measured decay and starvation deficit (two seeds, two decay rates)
the nutrient budget closes to round-off: on the grid is what was added minus what decayed, and added is supply minus eaten
density near the river is over ten times that of the eastern half; a resumed checkpoint is identical; same seed, same run

references: Grimm, V. and Railsback, S. F. (2005). Individual-based Modeling and Ecology. Princeton University Press.
Okubo, A. and Levin, S. A. (2001). Diffusion and Ecological Problems: Modern Perspectives, 2nd ed. Springer.

models.name: forest_fire
models.title: Forest fire and succession on a raster
models.summary: Fire spreading through a tree raster, with optional regrowth and lightning.

card.name: forest_fire
card.title: Forest fire and succession on a raster
card.summary: Fire spreads from the west edge through a raster of trees, with optional regrowth and lightning (Drossel-Schwabl); without them it is site percolation on the square lattice.
intended_use: Teaching percolation: how the burnt share jumps at the threshold density `p_c = 0.592746` of the square lattice.
Teaching self-organised disturbance regimes with regrowth and lightning switched on (the Drossel-Schwabl model).
A starting point for raster disturbance models, with a per-cell tree probability from a `cover` raster in place of a uniform density.
out_of_scope: Predicting the spread of a real wildfire: there is no wind, slope, fuel moisture, weather or fire suppression, and nothing is calibrated.
Fire-risk, evacuation or land-management decisions for a real place.
Questions about fire intensity or duration: a cell is empty, a tree, burning or burnt, and burns out in one step.
data: None by default: the 100 x 100 raster and the tree density of 0.6 are illustrative values in `ForestScenario`.
Optionally, a per-cell tree probability of shape `(width, height)`, for example the values of a `modelly.space.geo.RasterLayer`, passed as `cover`.
limits: Fire spreads to the four von Neumann neighbours of a burning cell with certainty, and every burning cell burns out after one step.
The fire starts from all trees on the west edge, so results describe a front crossing the raster, not ignition at a point.
Growth and lightning are constant probabilities per cell and step, with no age, species or seasons.
The validation covers the percolation case without growth and lightning; succession mode is only checked to keep burning and conserve cells.
ethics: Fire results can look like statements about real fire risk; this model has none of the physics of a real fire, so say it is illustrative whenever results are shown.

validation.check: at p_c - 0.15 the fire never reaches the east edge and burns under 10 % of the trees (three seeds)
at p_c + 0.15 the fire always reaches the east edge and burns over 90 % of the trees (three seeds)
the mean burnt share rises with density; a cover raster confines the trees; succession keeps burning and conserves cells; same seed, same fire

references: Drossel, B. and Schwabl, F. (1992). Self-organized critical forest-fire model. Physical Review Letters, 69(11), 1629-1632.
Newman, M. E. J. and Ziff, R. M. (2000). Efficient Monte Carlo algorithm and high-precision results for percolation. Physical Review Letters, 85(19), 4104-4107.
Stauffer, D. and Aharony, A. (1994). Introduction to Percolation Theory, 2nd ed. Taylor and Francis.

models.name: order_book
models.title: Continuous double auction (zero-intelligence order book)
models.summary: Random limit, market and cancel orders (per resting order) in a limit order book.

card.name: order_book
card.title: Continuous double auction (zero-intelligence order book)
card.summary: A limit order book on an integer price grid fed by random market, limit and cancel orders, in the zero-intelligence style of Farmer, Patelli and Zovko: no trader has a strategy, yet returns have fat tails.
intended_use: Teaching how a limit order book works: best quotes, the spread, market orders that take liquidity and limit orders that provide it.
Showing that a stylised fact (fat-tailed returns) can come from the mechanics of the book alone, with no strategic traders.
A starting point for order-book models, with a validated core to extend (order sizes, informed traders, other placement rules).
out_of_scope: Forecasting prices or returns of a real asset: the order flow is random and nothing is calibrated to market data.
Designing or testing trading strategies: there are no strategic traders, and the book does not respond to them as a real market would.
Claims about stylised facts beyond fat tails (volatility clustering, the shape of the spread distribution): the tests check only kurtosis and a valid book.
data: None by default: the price grid, the order rates and the initial depth are illustrative values in `OrderBookScenario`.
limits: Every order is one unit and limit prices are uniform within `window` ticks of the opposite best quote; real order sizes and placements are far from uniform.
Order flow is zero-intelligence: rates do not depend on prices, the spread or past returns.
A side is never emptied: an event that would remove its last order becomes a limit order on that side, which a real book does not guarantee.
Prices live on a fixed grid of `ticks` levels; limit orders that would fall outside it are clipped to its edges.
ethics: This is a toy market; results presented as evidence about a real market or a regulation (tick sizes, cancellation rules) would overstate what it shows.

validation.check: excess kurtosis of mid-price returns above five times its sqrt(24 / n) standard error under normal returns (three seeds)
the spread is at least one tick at every step and no level holds a negative number of orders
aggressive market orders never empty a side of a one-order book; same seed, same price path

references: Farmer, J. D., Patelli, P. and Zovko, I. I. (2005). The predictive power of zero intelligence in financial markets. PNAS, 102(6), 2254-2259.
Cont, R. (2001). Empirical properties of asset returns: stylized facts and statistical issues. Quantitative Finance, 1, 223-236.

models.name: kinetic_wealth
models.title: Boltzmann wealth exchange
models.summary: Random pairs pass one unit of money: the Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution emerges.

card.name: kinetic_wealth
card.title: Boltzmann wealth exchange
card.summary: Random pairs of agents pass one unit of money at a time; money is conserved and nobody goes into debt, yet equal shares turn into an exponential (Boltzmann-Gibbs) distribution of wealth.
intended_use: Teaching how inequality can emerge from random exchange alone, with equal agents and no skill or saving.
Comparing a simulated wealth distribution with an exact stationary law, as a worked example of validating a stochastic model.
A starting point for kinetic exchange models, with a validated core to extend (saving propensities, taxes, unequal exchange).
out_of_scope: Describing or forecasting the wealth distribution of a real economy: nothing is calibrated, and real distributions have Pareto tails this model lacks.
Arguing that real inequality is, or is not, deserved or random: the model has no production, work, inheritance or institutions.
Evaluating redistribution policies: there are no taxes, transfers or prices in the model.
data: None by default: the number of agents and the starting money are illustrative values in `KineticScenario`.
limits: Every exchange moves exactly one unit and every agent meets one random partner per step: no network, no geography, no preferences.
Money is conserved and the population is closed: no production, consumption, debt, births or deaths.
The validation is of the stationary law only; how fast equal shares spread out depends on the one-unit, one-matching-per-step rule.
ethics: Results can be read as saying inequality is natural or inevitable; the model shows only what random exchange does, so present it with the assumptions above.

validation.check: time-averaged Gini within three single-snapshot standard deviations of the exact stationary law's Gini, which is about one half (three seeds)
pooled wealth histogram closer to the exact marginal, in total variation, than one histogram of n independent draws (three seeds)
the exact marginal sums to one with mean `money`; money is conserved and never negative; same seed, same run

references: Dragulescu, A. and Yakovenko, V. M. (2000). Statistical mechanics of money. European Physical Journal B, 17, 723-729.

models.name: bouchaud_mezard
models.title: Bouchaud-Mezard wealth condensation
models.summary: Multiplicative returns plus exchange: an inverse-gamma wealth distribution.

card.name: bouchaud_mezard
card.title: Bouchaud-Mezard wealth condensation
card.summary: Each agent earns a random multiplicative return and exchanges with everybody at a mean-field rate; relative wealth settles to an inverse-gamma law with a Pareto tail that fattens as noise grows against exchange.
intended_use: Teaching how multiplicative returns concentrate wealth and how exchange between agents holds that concentration back.
Comparing inequality (the Gini coefficient) across noise-to-exchange ratios against an analytic stationary law.
A starting point for wealth models with multiplicative noise, with a validated core to extend (networks of exchange, taxes, heterogeneous returns).
out_of_scope: Describing or forecasting a real economy's wealth distribution: the rates are illustrative and nothing is calibrated.
Recommending tax or redistribution levels: the exchange term is a stylised mean-field pull, not a policy instrument.
Regimes with sigma^2 / J of 2 or more (shape alpha of 2 or less): the stationary law then has infinite variance and the tests do not cover it.
data: None by default: the number of agents, the exchange rate, the volatility and the step length are illustrative values in `BouchaudMezardScenario`.
limits: Mean-field exchange: every agent exchanges with the average of everybody, with no network or local structure.
Returns are independent across agents and in time, with the same volatility for everyone.
Wealth is reported relative to the mean, so growth of total wealth is not modelled; the step `dt` adds a small discretisation bias.
The validation is of the stationary Gini only, for sigma^2 / J = 0.5, 1 and 1.5, not of the time course.
ethics: Results can be read as saying wealth concentration is inevitable or that more exchange is the remedy; present them as properties of this stylised model, not of a real economy.

validation.check: time-averaged Gini within three single-snapshot standard deviations of the inverse-gamma law's Gini, for sigma^2 / J = 0.5, 1 and 1.5 (two seeds)
both the analytic and the simulated Gini rise with sigma^2 / J
shape alpha = 1 + 2 J / sigma^2; an unstable step is rejected; wealth stays positive with mean one; same seed, same run

references: Bouchaud, J.-P. and Mezard, M. (2000). Wealth condensation in a simple model of economy. Physica A, 282, 536-545.

models.name: deffuant
models.title: Deffuant bounded-confidence opinion dynamics
models.summary: Random pairs of agents compromise when their opinions are close enough.

card.name: deffuant
card.title: Deffuant bounded-confidence opinion dynamics
card.summary: Agents with opinions in [0, 1] meet in random pairs and compromise only when their opinions are within a confidence bound; a wide bound ends in consensus, a narrow one in several clusters.
intended_use: Teaching bounded confidence: how a single threshold on who listens to whom decides between consensus and lasting disagreement.
Exploring how the number of opinion clusters depends on the confidence bound, against the rule of thumb of about 1 / (2 epsilon).
A starting point for opinion-dynamics models, with a validated core to extend (networks, stubborn agents, heterogeneous bounds).
out_of_scope: Predicting real opinions, votes or polarisation: opinions are one abstract number and nothing is calibrated to survey data.
Designing interventions on a real population (moderation, messaging): the model has no media, networks or identities.
data: None by default: initial opinions are drawn uniformly on [0, 1], and the bound and other parameters are illustrative values in `DeffuantScenario`.
limits: One step is a sweep of a random perfect matching, about n / 2 meetings of the original one-pair-per-step model, so time is not in the original units.
Everybody can meet everybody: no social network or geography.
All agents share the same confidence bound and convergence parameter.
Cluster counts depend on how clusters are measured (a gap of half the bound, and clusters under `min_cluster_share` of the agents not counted).
ethics: Results can be read as saying that people with distant views cannot be reached; present them as a property of this stylised rule, not of a real population.

validation.check: epsilon = 0.4 ends in one cluster (three seeds)
epsilon = 0.1 leaves floor(1 / (2 epsilon)) = 5 clusters, plus or minus two (three seeds)
mean cluster count does not grow over epsilon = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4; the mean opinion is conserved; epsilon = 0 freezes opinions; same seed, same run

references: Deffuant, G., Neau, D., Amblard, F. and Weisbuch, G. (2000). Mixing beliefs among interacting agents. Advances in Complex Systems, 3, 87-98.

models.name: schelling_regions
models.title: Schelling segregation on real neighbourhoods
models.summary: Two groups move between census tracts when too few neighbours are like them.

card.name: schelling_regions
card.title: Schelling segregation on real neighbourhoods
card.summary: Schelling's segregation model with census tracts in place of grid cells: households of two groups move between the 41 tracts of Chittenden County, Vermont, when too few of their neighbours are like them.
intended_use: Teaching Schelling's result that mild preferences give strong segregation, on the topology of real neighbourhoods rather than a grid.
A starting point for segregation models over other regions, by passing any tract adjacency (`GeoSpace(regions).contiguity(...)`).
Comparing thresholds or group shares in relative terms through Duncan's dissimilarity index.
out_of_scope: Describing or predicting segregation in Chittenden County or any real place: only the tracts' adjacency is real; every tract has the same number of dwellings and the households are random.
Explaining why real households move: the model has one preference rule and no prices, incomes, housing markets or discrimination.
Judging any group, tract or community from its results.
data: The 41 census tracts of Chittenden County, Vermont, bundled from the U.S. Census Bureau's 2023 cartographic boundary file (public domain); source and checksum in `modelly/space/geo/data/NOTICE.md`.
Only their queen contiguity is used; capacity, density, group share and threshold are illustrative values in `SchellingRegionsScenario`.
limits: Every tract has the same number of dwellings; real tract sizes and populations are ignored.
A household sees all households of its own and adjacent tracts with equal weight, and all unhappy households move at once into random free dwellings, at no cost.
Two groups only, with one shared threshold; the run stops when everybody is happy, which says nothing about real time scales.
There is no closed form: validation is qualitative (segregation far above random allocation), not a quantitative match.
ethics: The tracts are real neighbourhoods where real people live; results must not be read as a statement about their residents or how they choose where to live.
Segregation results can be taken to blame one group or to suggest that segregation is natural or harmless; present them as the outcome of a toy preference rule, with the assumptions above.

validation.check: with threshold 0 nobody moves and the allocation never changes
at threshold 0.45, for three seeds, the final dissimilarity is more than five standard deviations above random allocation (30 random allocations) and more than twice its mean
mean dissimilarity grows from threshold 0 to 0.3 to 0.5, ending above 0.9
the 41 tracts form one connected, symmetric neighbourhood graph; households and dwellings are conserved; same seed, same moves

references: Schelling, T. C. (1971). Dynamic models of segregation. Journal of Mathematical Sociology, 1(2), 143-186.
Duncan, O. D. and Duncan, B. (1955). A methodological analysis of segregation indexes. American Sociological Review, 20(2), 210-217.

models.name: hegselmann_krause
models.title: Hegselmann-Krause bounded-confidence opinion dynamics
models.summary: Every agent moves to the mean opinion of those within its confidence bound.

card.name: hegselmann_krause
card.title: Hegselmann-Krause bounded-confidence opinion dynamics
card.summary: Every agent moves, all at once, to the mean opinion of those within its confidence bound; the population freezes into clusters after finitely many steps, one cluster for a wide bound. A step costs O(n log n).
intended_use: Teaching bounded confidence with synchronous averaging: how the confidence bound decides between consensus and frozen clusters.
Exploring how the number of opinion clusters falls as the confidence bound grows.
A starting point for opinion-dynamics models, with a validated core to extend (networks, stubborn agents, heterogeneous bounds).
out_of_scope: Predicting real opinions, votes or polarisation: opinions are one abstract number and nothing is calibrated to survey data.
Designing interventions on a real population (moderation, messaging): the model has no media, networks or identities.
data: None by default: initial opinions are drawn uniformly on [0, 1], and the bound and other parameters are illustrative values in `HKScenario`.
limits: Every agent hears every other agent within the bound: no social network, and everybody updates at the same time.
All agents share the same confidence bound; the dynamics are deterministic once the initial opinions are drawn.
The run stops when no opinion moves by more than `tolerance`, or after `steps` steps.
Cluster counts depend on how clusters are measured (a gap of half the bound, and clusters under `min_cluster_share` of the agents not counted).
ethics: Results can be read as saying that people with distant views cannot be reached; present them as a property of this stylised rule, not of a real population.

validation.check: epsilon = 0.3 settles into a single cluster and the run stops (three seeds)
epsilon = 0.05 and 0.1 leave more than two and at most 1 / (2 epsilon) clusters (three seeds)
the O(n log n) step matches the O(n^2) definition to 1e-12 on 200 agents over five steps
mean cluster count non-increasing over epsilon = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and one at 0.3; a zero bound stops after one step; same seed, same run

references: Hegselmann, R. and Krause, U. (2002). Opinion dynamics and bounded confidence: models, analysis and simulation. Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation, 5(3).

models.name: axelrod
models.title: Axelrod culture dissemination
models.summary: Neighbours on a grid copy cultural traits with a probability set by similarity.

card.name: axelrod
card.title: Axelrod culture dissemination
card.summary: Axelrod's model of the dissemination of culture: sites of a grid copy traits from neighbours with a probability set by their similarity, until the map freezes into regions of identical culture.
intended_use: Teaching how local convergence can produce global polarisation: one culture for few traits per feature, many regions for many.
Exploring the transition in the number of regions as traits, features or grid size change.
A starting point for social-influence models with a validated core to extend (noise, media, other networks).
out_of_scope: Describing or predicting real cultures, opinions or political views: features and traits are abstract integers with no measured meaning.
Drawing conclusions about real communities, migration or policy from the number or size of regions.
data: None by default: cultures are drawn uniformly at random, and grid size, features and traits are illustrative values in `AxelrodScenario` (the 10 x 10, five-feature setting of the original paper).
limits: A small square grid without wrapping, von Neumann neighbours only: sites at the edge have fewer neighbours, and nobody moves.
Traits are nominal and all features weigh the same; there is no noise, so the absorbing state is reached and kept for ever.
Validation is qualitative, against the original paper's regimes on a small grid; regions on larger grids and the exact transition point are not checked.
ethics: Results about polarisation or the persistence of minority cultures can be read as statements about real groups; present them as properties of an abstract rule, not of any society.

validation.check: on the 10 x 10, five-feature grid, two traits end in a single region for at least four seeds of five
thirty traits leave more than 25 regions in every one of five runs
the mean number of regions grows from two to fifteen to sixty traits
in the frozen map every bond has overlap 0 or all features; the interaction rule on hand-made pairs; same seed, same culture map

references: Axelrod, R. (1997). The dissemination of culture: a model with local convergence and global polarization. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 41(2), 203-226.
Castellano, C., Marsili, M. and Vespignani, A. (2000). Nonequilibrium phase transition in a model for social influence. Physical Review Letters, 85(16), 3536-3539.

models.name: nagel_schreckenberg
models.title: Nagel-Schreckenberg traffic
models.summary: Cars on a ring road accelerate, brake to the gap ahead and dawdle at random.

card.name: nagel_schreckenberg
card.title: Nagel-Schreckenberg traffic
card.summary: The Nagel-Schreckenberg cellular automaton: cars on a single-lane ring road accelerate, brake to the gap ahead and dawdle at random, and jams form on their own and travel backwards.
intended_use: Teaching the fundamental diagram of traffic: free flow below a critical density, jams above it, and how random dawdling lowers the peak flow.
A starting point for cellular-automaton traffic models with a validated core to extend (lanes, on-ramps, signals).
Comparing densities, speed limits or dawdling probabilities in relative terms.
out_of_scope: Predicting flows, speeds or travel times on a real road: cells, steps and dawdling are not calibrated to any road or driver population.
Road design or safety decisions: there are no lanes, junctions, vehicle types or crashes.
data: None by default: road length, density, speed limit and dawdling probability are illustrative values in `TrafficScenario`.
limits: One lane on a closed ring: no overtaking, entries, exits or junctions, and the number of cars is fixed.
Space and time are discrete (one cell, one step) and every car follows the same rule with the same speed limit and dawdling probability.
The exact checks hold away from the critical density `1 / (max_speed + 1)`, where transients are longest.
ethics: Results could be quoted in decisions about real roads that affect the people who use and live near them; present them as properties of an uncalibrated toy road, not as estimates for a real one.

validation.check: without dawdling the steady flow is exactly min(density * max_speed, 1 - density) at seven densities on both sides of the critical density
with dawdling the flow peaks at an interior density and falls steadily on the jammed branch
at low density the flow is density * (max_speed - dawdle) within five standard deviations of the mean of independent Bernoulli dawdles
cars never share a cell and never exceed the speed limit; impossible densities are rejected; same seed, same run

references: Nagel, K. and Schreckenberg, M. (1992). A cellular automaton model for freeway traffic. Journal de Physique I, 2(12), 2221-2229.

models.name: road_traffic
models.title: Traffic assignment on a real street network
models.summary: Random trips routed by shortest path over OpenStreetMap streets of Burlington.

card.name: road_traffic
card.title: Traffic assignment on a real street network
card.summary: All-or-nothing traffic assignment on the drivable streets of downtown Burlington, Vermont: random trips between junctions drive the shortest path by length, and the model counts the vehicles on every street segment.
intended_use: Teaching the assignment step of the four-step transport model and its link to edge betweenness.
Seeing which street segments shortest paths load most under uniform demand, on Burlington or on any strongly connected `RoadNetwork`.
A starting point for assignment models with a validated core to extend (real demand matrices, congestion, equilibrium assignment).
out_of_scope: Predicting real traffic in Burlington or elsewhere: demand is uniform over junctions, not measured, and nothing is calibrated against counts.
Decisions about real streets (closures, signals, one-way changes) without real origin-destination demand and congestion.
Networks much larger than a few thousand junctions: the model holds `n x n` arrays.
data: The drivable streets of downtown Burlington, Vermont, bundled from OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors, Open Database License 1.0), one-way streets kept one-way; source and checksum in `modelly/space/geo/data/NOTICE.md`.
Trips per step and run length are illustrative values in `RoadTrafficScenario`; origins and destinations are drawn uniformly among the junctions.
limits: All-or-nothing assignment: every trip takes the shortest path by length, with no congestion, travel times or route choice.
Uniform demand between every ordered pair of junctions; real trips start and end at homes, jobs and shops, not at junctions.
The network is the extract as of its pinned date, limited to its largest strongly connected part; streets outside the box do not exist for the model.
ethics: Segment flows on real streets can look like real traffic counts; never present them as such, since the demand behind them is invented.
Decisions about which streets carry traffic affect the people who live and work along them; say that demand is uniform and congestion absent whenever results are shown.

validation.check: the model's edge betweenness equals NetworkX's edge_betweenness_centrality on every segment, and its total is the number of segments on all shortest paths
for three seeds every simulated flow is within five binomial standard deviations of its expectation, and segments on no shortest path carry nothing
distances are NetworkX's and one-way streets make routes asymmetric; a network with unreachable junctions is refused; same seed, same flows

references: Brandes, U. (2001). A faster algorithm for betweenness centrality. Journal of Mathematical Sociology, 25(2), 163-177.
Girvan, M. and Newman, M. E. J. (2002). Community structure in social and biological networks. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 99(12), 7821-7826.
Ortuzar, J. de D. and Willumsen, L. G. (2011). Modelling Transport, 4th ed. Wiley.

models.name: bass_diffusion
models.title: Bass diffusion of innovation on a network
models.summary: Households adopt from advertising and from adopting neighbours.

card.name: bass_diffusion
card.title: Bass diffusion of innovation on a network
card.summary: Households adopt an innovation, rooftop solar for instance, from advertising and from adopting neighbours, either well mixed as in Bass's model or over a random network.
intended_use: Teaching the Bass diffusion curve and the roles of innovation (p) and imitation (q).
Showing how network structure changes diffusion: a sparse network adopts more slowly than the well-mixed curve.
A starting point for adoption models (solar, heat pumps) with a validated core to extend (subsidies, heterogeneous households, real networks).
out_of_scope: Forecasting real adoption of a product or technology: the default p and q are illustrative, not fitted to sales or installation data.
Decisions about subsidies or targeting real households without parameters and a network estimated on them.
Products that can be abandoned or bought repeatedly: adoption here is once and for ever.
data: None by default: the number of households, p, q, the step and the mean degree are illustrative values in `BassScenario`.
The network, when used, is a random graph drawn by the model (`households * degree / 2` random distinct pairs), not a measured social network.
limits: Every household has the same p and q; there are no prices, incomes, dwelling types or capacity limits.
Adoption is drawn once per step of length `dt`, so the curve carries an Euler discretisation error against the Bass equation.
The network is Erdos-Renyi-like with no clustering or communities beyond chance; real acquaintance networks are not represented.
Closed population: no new households and no abandonment.
ethics: Results on who adopts first could inform which households a programme targets; present them with the assumptions above, since the model knows nothing about who can afford an innovation.

validation.check: well mixed, for three seeds, the adoption share is within the Euler error plus five linear-noise standard deviations of the Bass equation at every step
a dense network (50 neighbours) stays within the same bound
a sparse network (4 neighbours) lags the well-mixed recursion by more than three standard deviations at mid-diffusion
adoption never reverts; unknown mixing is rejected; same seed, same curve

references: Bass, F. M. (1969). A new product growth for model consumer durables. Management Science, 15(5), 215-227.
